::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Ten genera, sorted by height and by whether the air rose in a lump or a sheet. The name tells you what the air was doing.
:::

## Height and shape

Clouds are categorized by their **altitude** and **morphology** (Latin roots: *Stratus* = layered, *Cumulus* = heaped/puffy, *Cirrus* = curl of hair, *Nimbus* = precipitating):

```{=html}
<figcaption><strong>Figure 1 | Cloud names are a coordinate system: which altitude band the cloud occupies, and what shape it takes there.</strong> The Latin roots do the rest of the work — <em>stratus</em> means layered, <em>cumulus</em> heaped, <em>cirrus</em> a curl of hair, <em>nimbus</em> precipitating — so <em>cirrostratus</em> is a high ice sheet and <em>stratocumulus</em> a low heaped layer. The bands are not arbitrary: they follow temperature, and above roughly $6\text{ km}$ the air is cold enough ($\approx -50^\circ\text{C}$) that clouds are made of ice crystals rather than droplets, which is why high clouds look fibrous instead of sharp-edged. Cumulonimbus (magenta) is the one family that breaks the scheme, because a single convective updraft can carry a parcel from the surface to the tropopause in minutes, where the anvil spreads out against the stable stratosphere.</figcaption>
</figure>
```


## Key takeaways

- A cloud name combines an altitude band with a shape: stratus is layered, cumulus heaped, cirrus fibrous, nimbus raining.
- The bands follow temperature: above about $6\text{ km}$ the air is near $-50^\circ\text{C}$ and clouds are ice, which is why high clouds look fibrous rather than sharp-edged.
- Cumulonimbus breaks the scheme because one convective updraft carries a parcel from the surface to the tropopause, where the anvil spreads against the stable stratosphere.
- The name tells you whether the air rose in a lump (cumuliform) or a sheet (stratiform), and how high it got.
